newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich calls Medicare moves his biggest mistake.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich calls Medicare moves his biggest mistake.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Friday his handling of Medicare reform was the biggest mistake he had made as a congressional leader since 1995.

In a televised election debate aired in his home district, the Georgia Republican said that, in retrospect, he should have sought President Clinton's support for changing Medicare and held public hearings on the future of the federal government's health insurance program for the elderly.
But Gingrich firmly blamed what he called falsehoods perpetuated by labor unions, the Democratic Party and Clinton himself for the damage Medicare has caused Republicans in this year's campaigns.

When asked by the moderator what he would have done differently during his two years as House speaker, Gingrich said, "I would have stopped the process, held public hearings and ensured that we had Bill Clinton's commitment to save Medicare."
Gingrich, formerly the House minority whip, became speaker in January 1995 after leading Republicans during the previous fall to their first takeover of Congress in 40 years.

Democrats have characterized Medicare reform attempts as a Republican ploy to cut taxes on the wealthy by reducing the elderly's benefits. Their approach appears to have been effective in many areas, especially Florida, where a large aged electorate is threatening traditional Republican dominance.

Gingrich said a national advertising campaign that began in September 1995 with funding from labor unions had sought to misrepresent Republican proposals. In fact, he said, the Republicans would raise Medicare spending from $4,800 annually per person over 65 of age to more than $7,000.
"We should have driven that home and gotten the president signed on to saving Medicare or not moved forward," he said.

"Once the unions decided and the Democratic National Committee decided, with the president's support, that they would say things that were false, we were in a mess that, frankly, took us the last year to dig our way out of."
The 53-year-old speaker debated millionaire businessman Michael Coles, his Democratic challenger in Georgia's 6th Congressional District, a largely conservative area in Atlanta's suburbs.
Coles, who has based his campaign on decrying partisan politics, is trailing Gingrich in local opinion polls by 14 percentage points.
